title: Where things are
verifiedBy: LLM review of the romanization, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The second case ending of the course, and the only one that never appears without a preposition in front of it — which is where its name, the prepositional, comes from. The everyday shape is -e on the end: stol → na stolé, magazín → v magazíne, rabóta → na rabóte, kómnata → v kómnate, Moskvá → v Moskvé.

v is roughly "inside" and na roughly "on" or "at", but which one a place takes is as often a fact about the word as it is about the geometry: v magazíne, but na rabóte — and nobody stands on top of their job. Learn each place WITH its preposition, the way you learn a noun with its gender.

yest' means "there is" — it asserts that something exists somewhere: Na stolé yest' kníga. When you already know the thing exists and are only saying WHERE it is, yest' drops out entirely: Kníga na stolé. That drop is the difference between announcing a book and locating one.

There is no dummy subject. English "there is a book on the table" has a "there" that means nothing and an "is" that agrees with the book; Russian has neither — na stolé yest' kníga is simply "on table is book". Reaching for a Russian word to put where "there" was is the trap, and there is none.
zdes' ("here") and tam ("there") take no preposition and no ending, so they answer Gde …? without touching the case system at all. They are the easiest answers on the rung.

Word order is already doing the work English gives to a and the. Kníga na stolé puts the known thing first and the news last: "THE book is on the table". Na stolé kníga turns it round: "there is A book on the table". Both are correct and they are not interchangeable — M10 makes this the lesson.

words.note: "Where", asking about a position rather than a direction. Russian has a second word for "where to" (kudá), which this level does not teach — M5's domóy covered the only direction the course needs.

sentences.trap: Two words, and no verb — the zero copula from M1 has been quietly running under every sentence since. "Where IS the book" has an is that Russian simply does not write in the present.
sentences.sound: gdye KNEE-ga. Russian is comfortable starting a word with g and d together; say both, quickly.

variations.changed: swap what is being looked for — the frame is two words either way
a full verb after Gde, and it takes the polite you-ending
a possessive word slips in front of the noun — moy agrees with what it describes

mistake.why: yest' asserts that something exists; it does not fill the gap where English puts is. Gde kníga? is the question.

sentences.usage: Looking for something — the most-used question on this rung.
sentences.mnemonic: Where plus the thing. Russian charges nothing for the "is", here as everywhere in the present.

sentences.cue: The book is on the table

words.note: "On" — and "at" for a place you think of as an activity rather than a container: na rabóte (at work), na póchte. It bends the word after it into the -e shape, as v does.
Table. stol is the dictionary shape and the subject shape; stolé is what v and na take. Masculine — it ends in a consonant — and the stress sits on the ending in both shapes: stol, sta-LYE.

sentences.trap: The answer to Gde …? is where the ending appears, not the question. stol is the shape you look up; stolé is the shape you stand things on.
sentences.sound: KNEE-ga na sta-LYE. The o of stolé is unstressed and flattens to "a", and the e on the end softens the l.

variations.cue: The newspaper is on the table
variations.changed: swap what is on the table — na stolé does not move

variations.cue: There is a book on the table
variations.changed: the same three words, reordered — and now the book is the news, not the table

variations.cue: The book is not on the table
variations.changed: ne in front of what it denies — here the place, since there is no verb

mistake.why: na bends the word after it. Standing on something is na stolé; na stol would be putting something onto it.

sentences.usage: Saying where a thing is — the plainest sentence this rung can make.
sentences.mnemonic: Look it up as stol, put things on it as stolé.

sentences.cue: There is a book on the table

words.note: "There is" — asserts that something exists, and never changes for number or gender: na stolé yest' kníga / knígi. Drops out when only saying where a known thing is: Kníga na stolé.

sentences.trap: The English sentence has four words of scaffolding — there, is, a — and Russian has none of them. yest' is not "is": it is the assertion that something exists, and putting it into Kníga na stolé would change what that sentence claims.
sentences.sound: na sta-LYE yest' KNEE-ga. yest' is one syllable ending soft; the ' is what softens the t.

variations.cue: There is a newspaper on the table
variations.changed: swap what exists — yest' does not move for gender or number

variations.cue: The book is on the table
variations.changed: drop yest' and reorder: now the book is known and its place is the news

variations.cue: There is bread in the shop
variations.changed: swap the place — the frame works with v as well as with na

mistake.why: The English "there" imported as tam, which means an actual other place. Russian's existential sentence has no dummy subject at all.

sentences.usage: Announcing that something is available — the sentence a shop assistant answers a question with.
sentences.mnemonic: yest' says a thing EXISTS. Where it is, is a different sentence.

sentences.cue: The bread is in the shop

words.note: Shop. Masculine, and it takes the same -e ending as stol: magazín → v magazíne. This is M4's v again, doing its other job — the clock seat and the place seat are one word with two lives.

sentences.trap: M4 taught v for the clock — v sem' chasóv — and it did not bend anything there. In front of a place it does. Same word, two jobs, and only one of them touches the ending.
sentences.sound: khlyep v ma-ga-ZEE-nye. The v here is barely a sound of its own; it leans onto the word after it.

variations.cue: The milk is in the shop
variations.changed: swap what is there — v magazíne is unchanged

variations.cue: There is bread in the shop
variations.changed: reordered with yest' — now it announces that bread is available
a verb instead of a bare noun — the place phrase is exactly the same

mistake.why: v bends the place after it, exactly as na does: v magazíne. v magazín would be going into the shop, not being there.

sentences.usage: Saying where something is kept or sold.
sentences.mnemonic: M4's v told the time and left the word alone. M7's v names a place and bends it.

words.note: "Here". No preposition, no ending, nothing to build — it answers Gde …? all by itself. The ' on the end is a silent softener — it is not a sound of its own, it is what makes the s before it soft.

sentences.trap: After a whole rung of endings, zdes' is a relief and a warning: not every answer to Gde …? is a bent noun. Some places are just words.
sentences.sound: KNEE-ga zdyes'. Another z and d together at the start, and the word ends soft.

variations.changed: swap the thing — zdes' never changes
zdes' → tam: the other end of the same pair
reordered with yest' — now it announces the book rather than locating it

mistake.why: zdes' is already a place. Putting a preposition in front of it is like saying "in here-place".

sentences.usage: Handing something over, or pointing at where it is.
sentences.mnemonic: Some answers to "where" are nouns with endings. Others are just zdes' and tam.

words.note: "There", meaning an actual other place — never the empty English "there" of "there is a book". That job belongs to yest', and mixing the two is the module's main trap.

sentences.trap: English uses "there" for two completely different things: a place ("the shop is there") and a piece of scaffolding ("there is a shop"). tam is only ever the first one.
sentences.sound: ma-ga-ZEEN tam. Note that magazín is back in its dictionary shape here — nothing is in front of it, so nothing bends it.

variations.changed: tam → zdes', the other end of the pair

variations.cue: There is a shop over there
variations.changed: the same two words reordered — now the shop is the news

variations.cue: The key is there, on the table
variations.changed: tam followed by the exact place, set off by a comma

mistake.why: One tam is a place and the other is English scaffolding. Russian needs only the first: Tam magazín.

sentences.mnemonic: tam is a place you could walk to. English's other "there" is nowhere at all.

words.note: Room. Feminine, and it takes the SAME -e ending as the masculine stol and magazín — this is the one case where the ending does not care about gender, which makes it much the easiest of the six.

sentences.trap: M3's object ending cared about gender: only feminine -a nouns became -u. This one does not. kómnata → kómnate and stol → stolé are the same ending on different genders.
sentences.sound: AN-na v KOM-na-tye. The stress stays at the front of kómnata in both shapes.

variations.changed: swap who is there — the place phrase does not move

variations.cue: There is a table in the room
variations.changed: reordered with yest' — and stol is back in its dictionary shape, being the thing that exists

variations.cue: Anna is not in the room
variations.changed: ne in front of the place, since there is no verb to put it in front of

mistake.why: -u is M3's object ending, for the thing a verb acts on. Being somewhere takes -e: v kómnate.

sentences.usage: Saying where a person is — and the sentence that shows this ending ignores gender.
sentences.mnemonic: One ending for all three genders. After M3, that is a gift.

words.note: Work, as a place and a thing — the noun behind M3's rabótat'. It takes na, not v, with no logic to recover: a Russian is on their work. Learn the preposition with the place.

sentences.trap: na normally means "on", and nobody stands on top of their job. This is the module's clearest case of the preposition being a fact about the word rather than about the world — and there are a dozen more like it.
sentences.sound: ee-VAN na ra-BO-tye. The unstressed a of rabóte flattens; the stress stays where it was in rabóta.

variations.changed: swap who — na rabóte is fixed
a pronoun subject, and still no verb in the sentence
ne in front of the place phrase

mistake.why: Work takes na, not v. There is no rule behind it — it is a fact about this word, and it has to be learned with it.

sentences.usage: Where somebody is during the day — one of the ten most-said sentences in the language.
sentences.mnemonic: v magazíne, but na rabóte. Learn the preposition with the place, not with the meaning.

sentences.cue: The key is on the table

words.note: Key. Masculine — it ends in a consonant sound — and it does not change here, because nothing is in front of it: only the word after a preposition bends.

sentences.trap: One noun bends and the other does not, in the same short sentence. stolé bends because na is in front of it; Klyuch does not, because nothing is in front of Klyuch.
sentences.sound: klyuch na sta-LYE. The ch is always soft in Russian, closer to the ch of "cheese" than of "chore".

variations.changed: a place that needs no preposition and no ending at all

variations.cue: There is a key on the table
variations.changed: reordered — now the key is the news and the table is what we already knew
the question this sentence answers

mistake.why: The ending belongs to the word after the preposition, not to the subject. Klyuch stays as it is.

sentences.usage: The most domestic sentence in the course — and the answer to the most domestic question.
sentences.mnemonic: Only what follows a preposition bends. Everything else stays as the dictionary has it.

words.note: "I live", from zhit' — pattern I, with yó in the you-form and the he/she-form: zhivyóte, zhivyót. The zhi at the front is always said "zhy" with a hard zh, whatever the spelling suggests.

sentences.trap: Moskvé is the third shape of a word M1 taught: Moskvá is the dictionary form, Moskvý is what iz takes, Moskvé is what v takes. All three live on one row, which is why tapping any of them opens the same note.
sentences.sound: ya zhy-VOO v mask-VYE. The i after zh is said as the hard y-vowel, not as an English "ee" — Russian's zh is always hard, and it hardens the vowel behind it.

variations.changed: swap the place — and Índii is the same shape iz took in M1, doing a second job
the polite you-form, with yó, after Gde
the he/she form — zhivyót, yó still in place

mistake.why: v bends the place after it. Moskvá is the dictionary shape; living there is v Moskvé.

sentences.usage: The line that follows Ya iz … in every introduction — where you are from, and where you are now.
sentences.mnemonic: Moskvá, Moskvý, Moskvé — one word, three jobs, one row.
